step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: The subject of this veterinary case report is a 1.5-year-old mixed-breed male dog, not a human patient.

step5_concept_grounding: Canine rabies in a domestic dog (veterinary case)

evidence_items.source_quote: The animal in this report was a mixed-breed male dog, aged approximately 1 year and 6 months from Belford Roxo, Rio de Janeiro state.

rationale: The subject of this case report is a 1.5-year-old mixed-breed male dog presenting with canine rabies, not a human patient. Under Step 2 and Step 3 of the annotation protocol, veterinary/animal cases are excluded from the human clinical gold standard benchmark → EXCLUDED_NON_HUMAN.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary human subject of case presentation, a 49-year-old female

step5_concept_grounding: Rabies vaccine-induced thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (adverse event following rabies immunization, not rabies viral infection)

evidence_items.source_quote: Questioning the patient's medical history, the patient was scratched by a cat on her left foot on March 28, and was vaccinated with a freeze-dried human rabies vaccine (Ningbo Rongan Biological Manufacturing Co., Ltd., drug batch number: National Medicine Standard S20073014) on March 28, April 4, April 6, and April 12, a total of 4 times.
She was initially diagnosed with rabies vaccination-related thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura based on clinical manifestations and examinations, ruling out other possible causative factors.

rationale: A 49-year-old woman received rabies vaccination after a cat scratch and developed thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) confirmed by positive ADAMTS13 inhibitory autoantibodies. Rabies is involved solely as a vaccination/immunization event causing an adverse reaction, not active viral infection. Under protocol rules, vaccine adverse event cases are non-target → EXCLUDED_NON_TARGET_CASE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject, a 23-year-old male presenting with horse bite crush injury

step5_concept_grounding: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis administered for animal bite trauma, not rabies viral disease

evidence_items.source_quote: Postexposure rabies prophylaxis (rabies immune globulin human 20 IU/kg) with the first-dose rabies vaccine was injected into the depth of the wound as well as around the wound. The remaining rabies immune globulin was injected into the deltoid muscle.

rationale: A 23-year-old male sustained a traumatic crush injury and fracture dislocation of his finger from a domestic horse bite. Rabies immune globulin and rabies vaccine were administered purely as post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). The patient never had rabies infection. Clinical role is PREVENTION_VACCINATION → EXCLUDED_NON_TARGET_CASE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject, a 5-year-old male child presenting with fatal rabies encephalitis

step5_concept_grounding: Clinical diagnosis of rabies encephalitis evaluated in case report

evidence_items.source_quote: A 5-year-old male child was bitten on the hands and face by a dog. Three doses of the antirabies vaccine were administered. One month after the bite, he presented with prodromal symptoms in the form of fever and malaise followed by altered sensorium, drowsiness, and irrelevant talking.
The findings were consistent with those described in prior reports of rabies encephalitis [Figures 1-5].
Considering the characteristic clinical presentation and rapid progression of the illness to death, laboratory confirmation of the disease was not obtained.

rationale: A 5-year-old boy presented with acute progressive fatal encephalitis and characteristic brainstem/thalamic MRI changes following a dog bite. Although clinically diagnosed with rabies encephalitis, the authors explicitly state that laboratory confirmation of the disease was not obtained. Under the universal claim eligibility rule and protocol guidelines, E3-only evidence (clinical/imaging findings without E1/E2 laboratory confirmation) cannot satisfy strict VPD → UNRESOLVED.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject, an 8-year-old male child presenting with aerophobia, hydrophobia, and encephalitis

step5_concept_grounding: Clinical diagnosis of furious rabies encephalitis evaluated in case report

evidence_items.source_quote: An 8-years-old male child presented in pediatric emergency with 5 days history of fever, altered sensorium, episodes of abnormal body movements, and agitation. Child had history of dog bite on face about 18 days back prior to admission, but he did not take any vaccination for that. He also showed features of aerophobia and hydrophobia.
There was rapid progression of symptoms and child died within 3 days of admission.

rationale: An 8-year-old boy presented with fever, agitation, hydrophobia, and aerophobia 18 days after an unvaccinated facial dog bite, with MRI showing brainstem/basal ganglia hyperintensities and rapid progression to death in 3 days. Under the Rabies evidence matrix, hydrophobia/aerophobia and imaging are classified as E3 supportive evidence; no E1 or E2 laboratory confirmation was obtained. E3-only evidence cannot satisfy strict VPD → UNRESOLVED.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject, a 35-year-old male farm worker with open forearm fracture from horse bite

step5_concept_grounding: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis administered for animal bite trauma, not rabies infection

evidence_items.source_quote: He was given 0.5 ml tetanus toxoid and 500 IU Tetglob  (human Tetanus Immunoglobulin BP), and received post-exposure rabies prophylaxis with Vaxirab  (Purified Duck Embryo Vaccine for Rabies IP).
The horse had no features of rabies.

rationale: A 35-year-old male sustained an open forearm fracture from a horse bite and received post-exposure rabies prophylaxis (Vaxirab). The horse showed no features of rabies, and the patient never developed rabies. Rabies appears solely as prophylactic vaccination → EXCLUDED_NON_TARGET_CASE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject (younger twin brother), a 19-year-old male presenting with serum sickness

step5_concept_grounding: Serum sickness adverse reaction following equine rabies immunoglobulin administration, not rabies viral infection

evidence_items.source_quote: According to an avulsion wound classified as category III in contexts of a contact with a suspected rabid animal, anti-rabies vaccine (SPEEDA , Liaoning Cheng Da Biotechnology, China) as a post-exposure strategy was initiated and oral amoxicillin/clavulanic acid was also prescribed for 3 days in terms of infection prophylaxis. After the skin sensitivity test on his right volar arm was negative, equine rabies immunoglobulin (TRCS ERIG , Queen Saovabha Memorial Institute, Thailand) was then administered around the wound site, and the remainder was administered intramuscularly into the left gluteal region.
A diagnosis of serum sickness was made and treatment with oral prednisolone (20 mg/day) and cetirizine (10 mg/day) was initiated for 7 days.

rationale: A 19-year-old male developed serum sickness following equine rabies immunoglobulin (ERIG) administered as rabies post-exposure prophylaxis for a cat scratch. The patient had an adverse reaction to foreign equine protein, not rabies virus infection. Discourse role is vaccine/immunoglobulin adverse reaction → EXCLUDED_NON_TARGET_CASE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject (elder twin brother), a 19-year-old male presenting with serum sickness

step5_concept_grounding: Serum sickness adverse reaction following equine rabies immunoglobulin administration, not rabies viral infection

evidence_items.source_quote: According to an abrasion wound with contact bleeding, anti-rabies vaccine (VERORAB , Sanofi Pasteur, France) was injected at his left deltoid. After the skin sensitivity test on his right volar arm showed negative results, equine rabies immunoglobulin (TRCS ERIG , Queen Saovabha Memorial Institute, Thailand) was infiltrated around the wound and intramuscularly into the left gluteal region.

In this case, prednisolone (30 mg/day) and cetirizine (10 mg/day) were given orally for 7 days. His fever resolved and skin lesions became light brown on day 7 of oral medication administration as shown in Figure 4.

rationale: A 19-year-old male developed serum sickness following equine rabies immunoglobulin (ERIG) administration for a cat scratch. No rabies infection occurred; the clinical claim concerns an immunological adverse reaction to equine immunoglobulin. Prevention/adverse event context → EXCLUDED_NON_TARGET_CASE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject, a 13-year-old boy with laboratory-confirmed rabies encephalitis who recovered

step5_concept_grounding: Diagnosis of Rabies encephalitis evaluated in case report

evidence_items.source_quote: The paired sera showed the antibody titers in excess of 1:60,000 dilution after 45 days of vaccine treatment confirming the diagnosis of rabies infection.

Subsequent to these results, other samples were collected from the nape of the neck and the cornea. The presence of the rabies antigen in the nerve twigs confirmed the diagnosis of rabies encephalitis. The confirmatory tests were conducted at the Department of Virology, Armed Forces Medical College (AFMC), Pune and the National Institute for Mental Health and Neurological Sciences (NIMHANS), Bengaluru.
evidence_items.specimen: nape of the neck and cornea biopsy

rationale: A 13-year-old boy presented with encephalopathy following a dog bite. Rabies virus antigen was detected in nerve twigs from a nape of neck/corneal biopsy (E1 confirmatory), and paired sera showed antibody titers > 1:60,000 (E2 strong evidence). Primary diagnosis of rabies encephalitis affirmed, current episode, primary patient, no contradictions. VPD fully satisfied → POSITIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject, a 25-year-old postpartum woman clinically diagnosed with rabies (baby boy is secondary subject)

step5_concept_grounding: Clinical diagnosis of rabies in a postpartum woman

evidence_items.source_quote: In May 2013, a 25-year-old, 4-month pregnant woman was bitten by a dog on the right instep when wearing slippers and walking on the Xiaoying village road.
On November 8, manifestations including hydrophobia, vomiting, madness, dysphagia and fear appeared. She was clinically diagnosed with rabies.
At 12:00 p.m. on November 9, the patient died at home in respiratory failure.

rationale: A 25-year-old woman developed classic manifestations of rabies (hydrophobia, dysphagia, agitation, death from respiratory failure) months after an untreated dog bite. Although clinically diagnosed with rabies, no laboratory confirmatory testing (E1/E2) was performed. Under the benchmark rules, E3-only supportive evidence cannot satisfy strict VPD → UNRESOLVED.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject of case 1, a 10-year-old boy presenting with paralytic rabies

step5_concept_grounding: Clinical diagnosis of paralytic rabies (dumb rabies)

evidence_items.source_quote: His past history elicited an incident of an unprovoked bite by a street dog in his right hand (grade III) three weeks back.
Four doses of purified chick embryo cell (PCEC) antirabies vaccine were administered according to schedule in the deltoid, starting from the day of the bite.
Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) was not given.
A serological test for rabies was not possible due to some technical difficulties.
They classified the case as being nonpolio and as paralytic rabies.

rationale: A 10-year-old boy developed acute flaccid paralysis progressing to bulbar palsy and death after a dog bite managed with vaccine without RIG. The National Polio Surveillance Expert Committee classified it as paralytic rabies, but laboratory serological testing was explicitly not possible due to technical difficulties. Without E1 or E2 laboratory confirmation, E3 supportive evidence is insufficient for strict VPD → UNRESOLVED.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject of case 2, a 6-year-old girl presenting with laboratory-confirmed paralytic rabies

step5_concept_grounding: Diagnosis of paralytic rabies evaluated in case report

evidence_items.source_quote: The CSF test was strongly positive for rabies antigen and immune complexes.
Neutralizing antibodies to rabies virus were detected in both serum and CSF by the Rapid Fluorescent Focus Inhibition Test (RFFIT).

rationale: A 6-year-old girl developed acute flaccid paralysis following a dog bite. CSF was strongly positive for rabies antigen (E1 confirmatory), and neutralizing antibodies were detected in both serum and CSF by RFFIT (E2 strong evidence). Primary diagnosis confirmed, current episode, primary patient, no contradiction. VPD fully satisfied → POSITIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Subject of this veterinary case report is an 11-year-old female spayed Labrador Retriever dog

step5_concept_grounding: Canine injection-site sarcoma following rabies vaccination in a dog

evidence_items.source_quote: An eleven-year-old female spayed Labrador Retriever was presented for evaluation of multinodular subcutaneous masses in the dorsal cervical area (Figure 1).
Three nonadjuvant vaccinations, DA2PP-Lepto, Rabies, and Bordetella, had been injected into this same area during a wellness examination three weeks earlier.

rationale: The subject is an 11-year-old female spayed Labrador Retriever dog that developed a grade 3 injection-site soft tissue sarcoma following routine vaccinations including rabies vaccine. Non-human animal case → EXCLUDED_NON_HUMAN.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Subjects of this case series are domestic shorthair cats (feline veterinary patients)

step5_concept_grounding: Veterinary meningoencephalomyelitis in cats; rabies virus IHC negative

evidence_items.source_quote: Immunohistology for feline parvovirus, feline coronavirus, feline herpesvirus, tick borne encephalitis virus, Borna disease virus, morbillivirus and rabies virus was negative in CNS parenchyma.

rationale: The subjects of this report are domestic cats with meningoencephalomyelitis of unknown origin, in which CNS immunohistochemistry for rabies virus was negative. Non-human animal case → EXCLUDED_NON_HUMAN.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject of case 1, a 3-year-old girl with facial laceration from dog bite

step5_concept_grounding: Rabies prophylaxis evaluation following dog bite trauma, not rabies disease

evidence_items.source_quote: Tetanus and rabies prophylaxis were evaluated. The child was reviewed after 1 week and sutures were removed (Fig. 3). The patient was kept on regular follow-up for 3 months.

rationale: A 3-year-old girl presented with facial lacerations from a stray dog attack. Rabies was considered strictly in the context of prophylaxis evaluation; the patient had no signs of rabies virus infection and healed completely. Prophylaxis/trauma context → EXCLUDED_NON_TARGET_CASE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject of case 2, a 13-year-old boy with facial laceration from dog bite

step5_concept_grounding: Rabies prophylaxis evaluation following dog bite trauma, not rabies infection

evidence_items.source_quote: Tetanus and rabies prophylaxis were evaluated. The child was reviewed after 1 week and sutures were removed (Fig. 6). The patient was kept on regular follow-up for 3 months.

rationale: A 13-year-old boy sustained a facial bite laceration from a stray dog. Rabies prophylaxis was evaluated as part of trauma care. No active rabies disease occurred. Prevention/prophylaxis context → EXCLUDED_NON_TARGET_CASE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject of case 3, a 6-year-old girl with infected dog bite wound

step5_concept_grounding: Rabies prophylaxis evaluation following dog bite trauma, not rabies infection

evidence_items.source_quote: Tetanus and rabies prophylaxis were evaluated. The child was reviewed after 1 week and sutures were removed. The patient was kept on regular follow-up for 3 months.

rationale: A 6-year-old girl presented with an infected dog bite wound on her cheek. Rabies prophylaxis was evaluated; the patient had no rabies infection and recovered uneventfully. Prophylaxis context → EXCLUDED_NON_TARGET_CASE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject, a 10-year-old girl with adverse reactions to rabies vaccination

step5_concept_grounding: Adverse drug/vaccine reaction following rabies vaccination, not rabies infection

evidence_items.source_quote: The child remains healthy a year later at review in clinic and did not develop any signs or symptoms of rabies.

rationale: A 10-year-old girl received rabies post-exposure prophylaxis following a dog bite in Bali and developed systemic adverse reactions (angioedema, hypotension) to the rabies vaccine. She never developed rabies infection. Vaccine adverse reaction context → EXCLUDED_NON_TARGET_CASE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject, a 36-year-old man with presumptive rabies who survived

step5_concept_grounding: Presumptive diagnosis of human rabies evaluated in case report

evidence_items.source_quote: A presumptive diagnosis of human rabies was made on the first day of admission.

Although the hospital lacked the capacity to perform basic tests that could isolate the viral antigens to help support the diagnosis of rabies virus in the patient, doctors informed the veterinary services and with the support of the relatives of the patient they located the buyer of the dog that bit him. The dog was still alive and then put to death. A confirmation of rabies infection was made by direct fluorescent antibody test on the dog's brain tissue.

rationale: A 36-year-old man presented with agitation, photophobia, and hydrophobia after a dog bite; the dog's brain was positive for rabies by DFA, but the hospital could perform no diagnostic tests on the patient himself. The patient survived completely with only diazepam and supportive care. Under protocol rules, animal diagnostic testing anchors to the animal, not the patient, leaving only E3 presumptive clinical evidence for the patient. E3-only evidence cannot satisfy strict VPD → UNRESOLVED.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject, an 18-year-old male with laboratory and autopsy confirmed paralytic rabies

step5_concept_grounding: Diagnosis of paralytic rabies confirmed post-mortem and antemortem

evidence_items.source_quote: Paralytic rabies was then suspected and rabies virus RNA was demonstrable in saliva but not in the urine by nucleic acid sequence based amplification technique (3).
The patient died after 12 days of hospitalization (15 days after first clinical onset). Autopsy findings showed wide spread Negri bodies through out the whole neural axis.

rationale: An 18-year-old male presented with pneumomediastinum and paralytic rabies. Antemortem testing demonstrated rabies virus RNA in saliva by NASBA (E1 confirmatory), and autopsy revealed widespread Negri bodies throughout the whole neural axis (E1 confirmatory gold standard). Primary diagnosis affirmed in current episode of primary patient. VPD fully satisfied → POSITIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject, a 3-year-old female child presenting with probable rabies

step5_concept_grounding: Diagnosis of probable rabies evaluated in case report

evidence_items.source_quote: She was managed as a case of 'probable rabies' with a differential diagnosis of bacterial encephalitis and septic encephalopathy.

On the third day of admission, she had the third episode of generalized tonic-clonic seizures and developed stridor with classic aerophobia, tachycardia (pulse rate 160/min) and tachypnoea (respiratory rate 70/min). Subsequently, she developed coma and despite adequate resuscitation, the child died on the fourth day of admission.

To confirm the diagnosis and evaluate for other causes of encephalitic syndrome, we did not have neuroimaging facilities (currently are not available in district hospitals) or rapid antigen tests for rabies on saliva or the cerebrospinal fluid.

rationale: A 3-year-old girl presented with fever, agitation, aerophobia, hypersalivation, seizures, and rapid progression to death following an unprovoked dog bite. She was managed as probable rabies, but the district hospital lacked rapid antigen testing, PCR, or neuroimaging facilities. Under the benchmark protocol, E3-only supportive evidence without E1/E2 laboratory confirmation cannot satisfy strict VPD → UNRESOLVED.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary human subject of post-mortem report, a reclusive man in his 80s

step5_concept_grounding: Speculative mention of rabies in forensic discussion of post-mortem scavenging by domestic dogs

evidence_items.source_quote: Since human and dog nervous tissue samples were inappropriate for post-mortem rabies diagnosis due to advanced putrefaction, rabies was not eliminated as the cause of death.

rationale: The report describes forensic investigation of an elderly recluse who died of natural causes/neglect and was scavenged by his dogs. Rabies was raised solely in speculative differential discourse and public health risk assessment due to putrefaction preventing testing. There is no patient-level evidence of rabies infection → EXCLUDED_NON_TARGET_CASE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject, a 14-year-old boy presenting with probable rabies after honey badger bite

step5_concept_grounding: Presumptive diagnosis of human rabies following wild honey badger bite

evidence_items.source_quote: On May 27, 2023, a 14-year-old boy from a rural area in Somalia came to the emergency room with complaining of agitation, high-grade fever, photophobia, and hydrophobia after a bite of a honey badger before four weeks.

A presumptive diagnosis of rabies was made, and the boy was admitted to the intensive care unit. Eight hours later, the vital signs and consciousness levels of the boy declined. After 48 hours in the ICU, he passed away. No more testing was carried out.

rationale: A 14-year-old boy presented with fever, agitation, photophobia, and hydrophobia 4 weeks after a wild honey badger bite that also killed his sister. He was presumptively diagnosed with rabies and died within 48 hours in the ICU. The authors note that no laboratory testing was carried out. Under benchmark criteria, E3-only clinical presentation without E1/E2 laboratory confirmation cannot satisfy strict VPD → UNRESOLVED.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject, a 17-year-old male with severe cranio-scalp trauma from lion attack

step5_concept_grounding: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis initiated following animal bite trauma, not rabies disease

evidence_items.source_quote: He received broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam) and tetanus prophylaxis. Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis was initiated after consultation with infectious disease specialists.

rationale: A 17-year-old male sustained severe cranio-scalp trauma from a pet lion attack and underwent complex surgical reconstruction. Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis was initiated preventively. The patient never developed rabies. Prophylaxis context → EXCLUDED_NON_TARGET_CASE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject, a 44-year-old male with ruptured gastric stromal tumor

step5_concept_grounding: Coincidental hemorrhage of a pre-existing gastric stromal tumor following rabies vaccine administration

evidence_items.source_quote: We present the case of a 44-year-old male who presented to the emergency department with mild and tolerable abdominal pain and distension 2 hours after receiving freeze-dried rabies vaccine (Vero-cells) for human use.

rationale: A 44-year-old male presented with acute hemoperitoneum caused by spontaneous hemorrhage of a giant gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) shortly after receiving a rabies vaccine injection. The primary condition is a neoplastic gastrointestinal disease; rabies vaccine was an incidental temporal trigger with no rabies infection. Discourse context → EXCLUDED_NON_TARGET_CASE.
